cards.statement: GitHub Issues links a sub-issue to a parent issue in a different repository.
cards.explanation: A parent issue can organize work from several repositories by adding existing issues as sub-issues.

cards.statement: Marking a GitHub notification as Done unsubscribes you from its conversation.
cards.explanation: Done removes a notification from the inbox while leaving the conversation subscription in place.
cards.misconception: Completing notification triage ends the subscription.

cards.statement: GitHub Projects auto-add workflows import matching existing items when first enabled.
cards.explanation: An auto-add workflow processes items when they are created or updated. Enabling it leaves existing matching items to be added separately.
cards.misconception: Enabling auto-add backfills the project's matching repository items.

cards.statement: GitHub Projects creates a repository issue when you add a draft issue to a project.
cards.explanation: A draft issue lives in its project. Converting it to an issue creates the repository-backed item.
cards.misconception: A project draft is already an issue in a repository.

cards.statement: Azure Boards links GitHub pull request titles containing AB# mentions to work items.
cards.explanation: Put AB# references in a pull request description to create Azure Boards links; titles do not create them.
cards.misconception: AB# linking accepts pull request titles as well as descriptions.

cards.statement: Azure Boards runs fixes AB#{ID} transitions when a GitHub pull request merges into the default branch.
cards.explanation: A merge into the repository's default branch activates recognized Azure Boards state transitions from pull request text.

cards.statement: Azure Boards displays GitHub pull request check status in a work item's Development section.
cards.explanation: Enabled pull request insights show passing, failing, or pending checks beside the linked GitHub pull request.

cards.statement: A YAML pipeline setting adds Integrated in build links to work items for code hosted in GitHub.
cards.explanation: With Automatically link new work items in this build enabled in an Azure Pipelines YAML pipeline's settings, each finished build adds an Integrated in build link to the Development section of its associated work items.

source.title: Link GitHub commits, PRs, branches, and issues to work items

cards.statement: Azure Boards can reject moving a work item into a column when its configured WIP limit is reached.
cards.explanation: Azure Boards treats WIP limits as soft constraints. Exceeding a column's limit highlights its count so the team can respond.
cards.misconception: WIP limits enforce a hard block on adding work to a full column.

cards.statement: Azure Boards measures lead time from a work item's first In Progress state to completion.
cards.explanation: Azure Boards lead time starts at work item creation; cycle time starts at the first In Progress state. Both end when the item reaches Completed.
cards.misconception: Lead time and cycle time use the same starting event.

source.title: Configure lead time and cycle time widgets

cards.statement: Azure Boards can create dashboard query charts from Tree of work items queries.
cards.explanation: Query-based charts use flat-list queries. A Tree of work items query serves hierarchical work item results instead.
cards.misconception: A tree query feeds query-based charts just like a flat-list query.

source.title: Azure DevOps dashboards and charts FAQs

cards.statement: Azure Boards query charts can aggregate Story Points with Sum when the field is in the query.
cards.explanation: Include Story Points in a query clause or column options, then use Sum to chart total estimates for the groups.

source.title: Track progress with status and trend query-based charts

cards.statement: Azure DevOps requires a query in Shared Queries before adding its chart to a dashboard.
cards.explanation: Saving the query in a Shared Queries folder makes its chart available to add to a dashboard.

source.title: Configure a chart for work items widget

cards.statement: View permission on an Azure DevOps dashboard is enough to see the charts of its query-based widgets.
cards.explanation: A dashboard viewer needs Read on the underlying query to see a query-based widget; without it, the widget shows a Widget failed to load message.
cards.misconception: Permission to view a dashboard shows every widget's chart regardless of query permissions.

source.title: Configure a chart for work items widget

cards.statement: Azure Boards velocity charts count work items in a Proposed state as Incomplete for their sprint.
cards.explanation: Velocity leaves Proposed items out of Completed, Completed Late and Incomplete; Incomplete covers items currently assigned to the sprint in an In Progress state.
cards.misconception: Any sprint item that has not reached Completed counts as Incomplete.

cards.statement: Azure Boards applies burndown report date edits to the sprint's iteration definition.
cards.explanation: Burndown report date controls change the displayed time window. The sprint's iteration dates remain separate.
cards.misconception: Editing the report's dates reschedules the underlying sprint.

cards.statement: The Test Results Trend (Advanced) widget displays results from several Azure Pipelines pipelines.
cards.explanation: Select multiple pipelines in the widget to track their test outcomes together over the chosen period.

source.title: Configure the Test Results Trend (Advanced) widget

cards.statement: Azure Pipelines' Pipeline pass rate report splits its daily failure trend by pipeline stage.
cards.explanation: The report's Failure trend counts failures per day and divides that data by stage when several stages apply, while Top failing tasks points to the failed runs.

cards.statement: Azure DevOps automatically refreshes a code wiki's pages from commits to its mapped branch and folder.
cards.explanation: The published code wiki follows the head of its mapped branch and folder, so committed documentation changes appear there.

source.title: Publish Git repository files to a wiki

cards.statement: Azure DevOps wiki can render a Mermaid process diagram from a fenced code block.
cards.explanation: An Azure DevOps wiki renders diagrams from fenced blocks with the mermaid language identifier.

cards.statement: Azure DevOps README files can render Markdown task lists as interactive checkboxes.
cards.explanation: Azure DevOps renders Markdown task-list checkboxes in wiki pages and pull request content; README files lack that support.
cards.misconception: README rendering supports the same Markdown features as wiki rendering.

cards.statement: GitHub uses pull request labels to categorize changes in generated release notes.
cards.explanation: GitHub release-note configuration maps pull request labels to categories, allowing a changelog to group changes by purpose.

cards.statement: Azure DevOps wiki Markdown embeds the results of an Azure Boards query in a page through the query's ID.
cards.explanation: Wiki Markdown takes query-table followed by a query ID inside a ::: block and renders that Azure Boards query's results as a table in the page.

source.title: Markdown syntax for files, widgets, and wikis

cards.statement: Azure DevOps buffers new service hook events while a subscription is on probation.
cards.explanation: A service hook subscription on probation loses new events; Azure DevOps retries the failed notification instead.
cards.misconception: Probation preserves new matching events in a backlog for delivery after the subscription recovers.

cards.statement: Azure Boards converts an existing OAuth repository connection in place when it moves to the GitHub App.
cards.explanation: To reconnect an Azure Boards repository through the GitHub App, remove it from its existing OAuth connection first.
cards.misconception: Installing the GitHub App converts an existing OAuth repository connection in place.

source.title: Install the Azure Boards App for GitHub

cards.statement: The Azure Boards app turns a Microsoft Teams channel conversation into a work item.
cards.explanation: The Azure Boards app creates work items from Microsoft Teams channel conversations, keeping feedback close to the discussion.

source.title: Use Azure Boards in Microsoft Teams

cards.statement: The Azure Boards app sends work item subscription notifications to Microsoft Teams direct messages.
cards.explanation: Azure Boards work item subscriptions deliver Microsoft Teams notifications in channels; chat and direct messages are unsupported.
cards.misconception: The Azure Boards app supports personal direct-message destinations for work item subscriptions.

source.title: Use Azure Boards in Microsoft Teams

cards.statement: Microsoft's branching guidance for Azure Repos starts each new feature branch from the main branch.
cards.explanation: Starting from main gives the feature branch the current integrated codebase.

cards.statement: The Azure Repos branching guide ports release fixes to main by merging the entire release branch.
cards.explanation: The documented porting workflow cherry-picks selected fixes, avoiding release-specific changes.
cards.misconception: Porting a release fix uses a full release-branch merge.

cards.statement: Azure Repos counts a pull request creator's approval toward the minimum reviewer count by default.
cards.explanation: The creator's approval counts toward the minimum when Allow requestors to approve their own changes is enabled.
cards.misconception: A creator's vote counts toward the minimum automatically.

cards.statement: Azure Repos can clear Wait votes with Reset all approval votes when contributors push source changes.
cards.explanation: Reset all approval votes preserves Wait and Reject votes when new source changes arrive.
cards.misconception: Resetting approval votes also clears votes to wait.

cards.statement: Azure Repos assigns separate policy bypass permissions for pull request completion and direct pushes.
cards.explanation: A permission to bypass policies during PR completion grants a different capability from bypassing policies during pushes.

cards.statement: GitHub combines overlapping rulesets using the most restrictive version of a shared rule.
cards.explanation: Layered protections aggregate; a weaker setting in another ruleset does not relax the stronger rule.

cards.statement: GitHub reserves access to view active repository rulesets for repository administrators.
cards.explanation: People with repository read access can inspect active rulesets.
cards.misconception: Viewing branch restrictions requires administrative access.

cards.statement: GitHub lets a repository administrator add a specific GitHub App to a ruleset's bypass list.
cards.explanation: A ruleset can grant a named GitHub App an exception to its protections.

cards.statement: Azure Repos automatically queues build validation when a contributor creates a draft pull request.
cards.explanation: Draft PRs use manually queued build validation rather than automatically running build validation policies.
cards.misconception: Draft pull requests trigger automatic policy builds.

cards.statement: Azure Repos supports SSH access to repositories that contain Git LFS-tracked files.
cards.explanation: Use HTTPS for Azure Repos repositories containing Git LFS-tracked files; Azure Repos does not support SSH for them.
cards.misconception: Git LFS repositories in Azure Repos support the same transports as ordinary Git repositories.

source.title: Manage and store large files in Git

cards.statement: Azure Repos stores a binary dragged into its web interface as a Git LFS pointer.
cards.explanation: Dragging a binary into the Azure Repos web interface commits its content to Git, rather than storing a Git LFS pointer.
cards.misconception: The Azure Repos web uploader applies Git LFS storage automatically.

source.title: Manage and store large files in Git

cards.statement: Scalar schedules background repository maintenance to improve work with large repositories.
cards.explanation: Scalar configures scheduled Git maintenance so expensive repository upkeep runs in the background.

cards.statement: A Git subtree merge automatically imports later upstream changes into the consuming repository.
cards.explanation: A subtree merge imports shared code into a repository, but engineers explicitly fetch and merge later upstream changes.
cards.misconception: A subtree merge establishes an ongoing synchronization relationship with upstream code.

cards.statement: Azure Repos grants history rewriting through the Contribute repository permission.
cards.explanation: Azure Repos uses Force push for rewriting history. Contribute authorizes ordinary contributions, rather than history replacement.
cards.misconception: Contribute includes the authority to overwrite existing repository history.

cards.statement: The Azure Repos web portal creates annotated tags rather than lightweight tags.
cards.explanation: The web portal creates only annotated tags, which record the tagger, message and date; lightweight tags come from the Git command line or Visual Studio.

cards.statement: Purging a file from GitHub repository history changes commit IDs further along that history.
cards.explanation: A GitHub history cleanup changes the affected commit and later commit hashes, which can disrupt automation that stores those IDs.

source.title: Removing sensitive data from a repository

cards.statement: git pull cleans purged sensitive data from an existing clone after GitHub history is rewritten.
cards.explanation: GitHub warns that pulling then pushing an old clone can reintroduce purged data. Collaborators need to clean or replace the clone.
cards.misconception: Pulling rewritten remote history purges the tainted history from an existing clone.

source.title: Removing sensitive data from a repository

cards.statement: Azure Repos lets engineers configure permission inheritance separately for individual repositories.
cards.explanation: Turning a repository's Inheritance setting off stops project-level Git permissions flowing into that repository.

cards.statement: Publishers send new Azure Artifacts package versions directly to the @release view.
cards.explanation: Publish packages to the base feed, then promote chosen versions to @release.
cards.misconception: A release view is a publication endpoint.

cards.statement: Azure Artifacts automatically saves upstream packages a Feed and Upstream Reader (Collaborator) installs via the feed.
cards.explanation: The Feed and Upstream Reader (Collaborator) role includes saving installed upstream packages into the feed.

cards.statement: Azure Artifacts checks upstream sources before packages published directly to the feed.
cards.explanation: Azure Artifacts checks directly published packages, then saved upstream packages, then packages available upstream.
cards.misconception: Configured upstream sources take precedence over locally published packages.

cards.statement: Azure Artifacts keeps a version reserved after you delete the published package.
cards.explanation: Azure Artifacts keeps a deleted package's version reserved. Publish changed contents under a new version.

cards.statement: Azure Artifacts feed views identify whether a package change breaks API compatibility.
cards.explanation: Azure Artifacts views communicate validation quality. SemVer communicates the nature and risk of a change.
cards.misconception: Feed views carry the compatibility meaning of semantic version numbers.

cards.statement: Azure Pipelines automatically resets $(Rev:r) when a date-based run number's date changes.
cards.explanation: Azure Pipelines restarts the revision when the date changes in a run number such as $(Date:yyyyMMdd).$(Rev:r).

cards.statement: GitHub Packages adopts repository permissions by default when you link an already published container package.
cards.explanation: Linking a published package in GitHub Packages preserves existing access rules. Enable inheritance to adopt repository access.
cards.misconception: Linking a published package automatically switches its access rules to the repository's.

cards.statement: Azure Artifacts can accept a new publication of a version present in an enabled upstream source.
cards.explanation: For Azure Artifacts, disable the relevant upstream before publishing a version it already contains; re-enable it afterward.
cards.misconception: An enabled upstream permits local publication of its existing package versions.

cards.statement: Azure Artifacts guidance ranks an upstream of internally customized OSS above public registries.
cards.explanation: Microsoft's Azure Artifacts guidance puts public registries first, except that an upstream with internally customized OSS packages takes priority.

cards.statement: Azure Pipelines' Publish Test Results task extracts results from a Docker build image.
cards.explanation: For tests executed during a Docker build, export result files to the pipeline host before publishing them.
cards.misconception: Test-result publishing extracts files stored in a built container image directly.

cards.statement: Azure Pipelines' Visual Studio Test task can balance test slices using past execution times.
cards.explanation: Execution-time slicing groups tests so each slice has approximately equal expected duration across the agents.

source.title: Run tests in parallel using the Visual Studio Test task

cards.statement: Azure Pipelines shows Code Coverage tab results while deployment stages run in a multistage YAML pipeline.
cards.explanation: The Code Coverage tab's results become available after the whole multistage YAML pipeline completes, delaying that coverage review until the run ends.
cards.misconception: A completed build stage exposes the Code Coverage tab's results while downstream stages remain active.
cards.volatilityNote: The timing of coverage reporting can change as Azure Pipelines evolves.

source.title: Review and configure code coverage results in Azure Pipelines

cards.statement: Azure Load Testing stops a running test by default when its error percentage crosses a threshold in a time window.
cards.explanation: Auto stop guards against costs from failing tests, such as a wrong endpoint URL; the YAML test configuration can tune errorPercentage and timeWindow or set autoStop: disable.

cards.statement: Azure Load Testing can execute a k6 script as a pipeline's load test.
cards.explanation: Azure Load Testing runs Apache JMeter or Locust scripts; k6 scripts use another test framework.
cards.misconception: Azure Load Testing accepts k6 scripts as well as its supported framework scripts.
cards.volatilityNote: The frameworks supported by Azure Load Testing can expand.

cards.statement: Azure Pipelines runs the Manual Validation task in an agentless job.
cards.explanation: The Manual Validation task pauses a YAML run within a stage and executes in a server job rather than occupying an agent.

cards.statement: Azure Pipelines Test Impact Analysis includes newly added tests in its selected test set.
cards.explanation: Test Impact Analysis includes new tests in its selection so incremental validation exercises tests introduced by the change.

source.title: Speed up testing by using Test Impact Analysis

cards.statement: Azure Pipelines requires an interactive process for visible UI tests on self-hosted Windows agents.
cards.explanation: Visible UI tests run on self-hosted Windows agents configured as interactive processes with autologon, providing an accessible desktop session.

cards.statement: Azure Pipelines fails the Publish Test Results task by default when a reported test fails.
cards.explanation: The Publish Test Results task publishes failing outcomes by default. Enable failTaskOnFailedTests to make reported failures fail the task.
cards.misconception: Publishing a failed test outcome fails the publication task under its default settings.

cards.statement: Azure Pipelines assigns a fresh virtual machine per job using Microsoft-hosted agents.
cards.explanation: A Microsoft-hosted job starts with clean machine state; local changes from an earlier job stay with that earlier machine.

cards.statement: Microsoft-hosted agents can reach a corporate network through its ExpressRoute private connection.
cards.explanation: Microsoft-hosted agents contact corporate servers over public networking. ExpressRoute and VPN connections do not give these agents a private route.
cards.misconception: Hosted agents use the organization's private Azure network connections.

cards.statement: Managed DevOps Pools can provision agents from custom generalized Azure Compute Gallery images.
cards.explanation: An engineer selects a generalized image from Azure Compute Gallery when the pool needs a prepared software environment.

cards.statement: The Azure Pipelines GitHub App runs builds as the GitHub user who installs the app.
cards.explanation: GitHub App authentication runs builds and reports status under the Azure Pipelines identity, rather than the installer's personal identity.
cards.misconception: The GitHub App delegates builds to its installer's personal identity.

cards.statement: Azure Pipelines adds explicit GitHub branch triggers to the pipeline's existing implicit CI trigger.
cards.explanation: An explicit trigger replaces Azure Pipelines' implicit CI trigger for a GitHub repository; configured branch filters determine which pushes start runs.
cards.misconception: Explicit branch filters supplement the implicit trigger instead of replacing it.

cards.statement: Azure Pipelines can reevaluate ${{ }} expressions after a task changes a variable in the same run.
cards.explanation: Azure Pipelines resolves template expressions while it compiles the YAML plan. Task-time variable updates leave those resolved values unchanged.
cards.misconception: Template expressions refresh their values during task execution.

cards.statement: Azure Pipelines can enforce an extends relationship through a resource's required template check.
cards.explanation: The required template check verifies that the pipeline extends the named template; including that file inserts content but does not meet the check.

cards.statement: Azure Pipelines reads an environment's approvals and checks from the pipeline author's YAML file.
cards.explanation: Resource administrators configure approvals and checks separately from YAML. Editing the pipeline file leaves the environment's check configuration intact.
cards.misconception: Pipeline authors define environment approvals and checks in YAML.

cards.statement: Azure Pipelines checks a secret-bearing variable group's authorization for the consuming pipeline.
cards.explanation: Naming a secret-bearing variable group in YAML does not authorize its use; the pipeline needs a matching library authorization.

cards.statement: Azure Pipelines deployment jobs inherit the implicit checkout: self behavior of regular jobs.
cards.explanation: Azure Pipelines uses checkout: none when a deployment job omits checkout. Add checkout: self to fetch the pipeline's source repository.
cards.misconception: Deployment jobs receive the same implicit source checkout as ordinary jobs.

cards.statement: Azure Pipelines injects artifact downloads into a deployment job's deploy hook by default.
cards.explanation: The deploy lifecycle hook receives an implicit artifact download step. Set download: none in that hook when the deployment uses another artifact source.

cards.statement: Azure Pipelines accepts the rolling strategy for Kubernetes resources in an environment.
cards.explanation: Azure Pipelines rolling deployments target virtual machine resources. A Kubernetes environment resource does not enable that deployment-job strategy.
cards.misconception: The rolling deployment-job strategy works with Kubernetes environment resources.

cards.statement: Azure Pipelines combines deployments from multiple pipelines in an environment's deployment history.
cards.explanation: An environment's deployment record identifies the pipeline and run behind a change, so releases from separate services remain traceable together.

source.title: Create and target Azure DevOps environments for pipelines

cards.statement: Azure Pipelines repeats configured postRouteTraffic health checks at successive canary increments.
cards.explanation: The canary strategy runs preDeploy once, then repeats deploy, routeTraffic and postRouteTraffic for each increment, so health checks recur as exposure grows; it ends with on: success or on: failure.

cards.statement: Azure Pipelines defaults postRouteTraffic to a server job for deployments that use an agent pool.
cards.explanation: Azure Pipelines runs lifecycle hooks in the deployment job's pool unless the hook sets another pool. A postRouteTraffic health check follows that inherited setting.
cards.misconception: Post-deployment health-check hooks select an agentless server job implicitly.

cards.statement: Azure App Configuration's targeting filter checks the user ID and groups that the app supplies in a targeting context.
cards.explanation: The feature flag stores the audience; the app says who the user is. In ASP.NET Core the default accessor uses the signed-in user name as UserId and Role claims as Groups.

source.title: Roll out features to targeted audiences in an ASP.NET Core app

cards.statement: Azure App Configuration lets percentage allocation override explicit user assignments in variant flags.
cards.explanation: A variant's explicit user or group assignment overrides its percentage allocation. A named tester can receive the selected variant regardless of the allocation bucket.
cards.misconception: Percentage allocations outrank named user overrides in variant feature flags.

cards.statement: Azure Pipelines starts an application stage under its default condition after its database stage dependency fails.
cards.explanation: The default Azure Pipelines stage condition expects its dependencies to succeed. An application stage therefore skips when its database deployment dependency fails.
cards.misconception: Waiting for a dependency to finish is sufficient for the default stage condition, regardless of its outcome.

cards.statement: Azure Resource Manager what-if computes utcNow() and newGuid() values when it previews a deployment.
cards.explanation: What-if can't evaluate nondeterministic functions such as utcNow() and newGuid() outside a deployment, so it shows the expression as-is and can report a change.
cards.misconception: What-if computes every template expression before comparing the template with live resources.

source.title: Bicep what-if: Preview changes before deployment

cards.statement: Azure Resource Manager leaves properties omitted from a template unchanged in an incremental redeployment.
cards.explanation: Incremental deployment reapplies all of a resource's properties, so properties omitted from the template are reset to their default values; specify every non-default value.
cards.misconception: Incremental deployment treats omitted resource properties as unchanged values.

cards.statement: Azure Resource Manager deploys an ARM template's resources in their listed order by default.
cards.explanation: Azure Resource Manager follows the dependency graph rather than file order. Independent resources deploy in parallel.
cards.misconception: The order of resource declarations determines the deployment order.

source.title: Define the order for deploying resources in ARM templates

cards.statement: Azure Resource Manager can record preflight validation failures in the activity log.
cards.explanation: Preflight validation errors appear in the activity log but have no entry in deployment history because deployment has yet to start.

cards.statement: The ARM template test toolkit's URI check can accept https://management.azure.com as a literal variable value.
cards.explanation: The toolkit flags hardcoded environment endpoints. Use the environment() function so a template adapts to the target Azure cloud.
cards.misconception: A valid Azure endpoint is accepted as a hardcoded value by the toolkit's URI check.

cards.statement: Azure Machine Configuration can apply operating system settings to Azure Arc-enabled servers.
cards.explanation: Azure Machine Configuration manages guest settings on Azure machines and hybrid machines connected through Azure Arc.

cards.statement: Azure Policy reports Azure Machine Configuration compliance from a VM's provisioningState value.
cards.explanation: Azure Policy reads complianceStatus from the guest assignment resource. A VM's successful provisioning state does not establish guest configuration compliance.
cards.misconception: VM provisioning success determines the guest configuration's compliance status.

cards.statement: Azure Machine Configuration reapplies settings in Apply and Monitor on in-scope VM tag edits with enforcement enabled.
cards.explanation: Enabled Azure Policy enforcement applies configuration when the machine resource changes. Updating an in-scope VM's Azure tag triggers that behavior.

cards.statement: Azure Machine Configuration uses policy metadata to create guest assignments for targeted machines.
cards.explanation: Definitions in the Guest Configuration category include guestConfiguration metadata. Azure Machine Configuration uses it to provision the machine's guest assignment.

cards.statement: Azure Pipelines can reference a classic task group from a YAML pipeline during migration.
cards.explanation: Task groups belong to classic pipelines. Reuse equivalent steps through a YAML template when migrating to YAML.
cards.misconception: YAML pipelines consume existing classic task groups.

cards.statement: Azure Pipelines exports a classic build designer's pipeline definition to YAML for migration.
cards.explanation: A pipeline created with the classic build designer supports YAML export. Classic release pipelines instead need their tasks exported individually.

source.title: Migrate your Classic pipeline to YAML

cards.statement: Azure Pipelines applies an organization-level run-retention policy across its projects.
cards.explanation: Azure Pipelines run-retention rules apply at project scope. Projects configure their own rules for pipeline runs.
cards.misconception: A central organization policy controls pipeline run retention across projects.

cards.statement: A script in an Azure Pipelines run can add a retention lease to that same run through the Lease API.
cards.explanation: A script in the pipeline calls the Lease API with the predefined run and definition IDs, so a production deployment run can be kept longer than a test run.

cards.statement: Azure Pipelines preserves published pipeline artifacts when retention deletes their producing run.
cards.explanation: Deleting an Azure Pipelines run also removes its pipeline artifacts. Preserve the producing run when downstream consumers still need those files.
cards.misconception: Published pipeline artifacts survive deletion of their producing run.

cards.statement: Azure Pipelines lets target-branch CI runs restore caches created under a pull request's merge-ref scope.
cards.explanation: Azure Pipelines places caches created by pull request validation in the merge-ref scope. Target-branch CI runs cannot read that scope, even when the cache key matches.
cards.misconception: Target-branch CI runs can read caches created in a pull request's intermediate merge branch.

cards.statement: Azure Pipelines can queue jobs despite idle self-hosted agents when parallel-job capacity is exhausted.
cards.explanation: Registering self-hosted agents does not increase an organization's parallel-job capacity. Jobs need available capacity as well as an available agent.

source.title: Configure and pay for parallel jobs

cards.statement: Once Azure Pipelines marks a test flaky, all pipelines for that branch see its flaky status.
cards.explanation: Flaky test management keeps flakiness data per branch, so all pipelines for that branch show the test's Flaky tag when teams troubleshoot failures.

cards.statement: Azure Pipelines saves a new cache as soon as the Cache task finishes restoring dependencies.
cards.explanation: Azure Pipelines saves a new cache during Post-job: Cache after the job's steps succeed. Restoring a cache earlier in the job is a separate operation.
cards.misconception: The Cache task saves new cache contents during its restore step.

cards.statement: Several self-hosted agent VMs in Azure share one user-assigned managed identity and its role assignments.
cards.explanation: A user-assigned managed identity is a standalone Azure resource with its own lifecycle, so agent VMs that are recycled often keep consistent role assignments.

cards.statement: A full-scoped Azure DevOps PAT can run operations that are denied to the user who owns it.
cards.explanation: A PAT can't grant more permissions than its owner has, whatever its scopes; the token works with the owner's current permissions.
cards.misconception: A full-scoped PAT carries its own permissions that bypass the owner's denies.

cards.statement: An Allow permission on a security group gives a Basic user test case management in Azure Test Plans.
cards.explanation: Test case management comes with Basic + Test Plans or an applicable Visual Studio subscription; to give a user such features, change the access level, not permissions.
cards.misconception: Security-group permissions can unlock features that the user's access level lacks.

cards.statement: A Stakeholder can act on assigned release approvals in a private Azure DevOps project.
cards.explanation: Stakeholder access includes viewing releases and acting on approvals. An engineer can involve a business approver through that access level.

cards.statement: Azure Pipelines uses project-level service connection roles to authorize edits after cross-project sharing.
cards.explanation: Once a service connection is shared, updates require an organization-level Administrator role in that connection's user permissions.
cards.misconception: Project-level service connection administration remains sufficient for editing a shared connection.

cards.statement: An organization owner can limit a GitHub App installation to selected private repositories.
cards.explanation: Selecting repositories narrows the installation's repository scope; the app uses its granted permissions within those repositories.

cards.statement: GitHub requires organization membership for a contractor to hold a repository's Admin role.
cards.explanation: GitHub can assign an outside collaborator any base repository role, including Admin, while keeping them outside the organization.
cards.misconception: A repository administrator must also be a member of its owning GitHub organization.

cards.statement: GitHub can count a Triage user's approval toward a repository's required approving reviews.
cards.explanation: GitHub lets Triage users submit reviews, but required approving reviews come from users with Write, Maintain or Admin access.
cards.misconception: Submitting an approving review makes it eligible to satisfy required reviews regardless of repository role.

cards.statement: Azure DevOps team administrators select the area paths that populate their team's backlog.
cards.explanation: Team administrators configure which project area paths appear on the team's backlogs and boards.

source.title: Define area paths and assign to a team

cards.statement: Azure Pipelines fetches linked Azure Key Vault secret values at runtime for the consuming pipeline run.
cards.explanation: A linked variable group holds selected secret names; a run retrieves their latest values from the vault.

source.title: Link a variable group to secrets in Azure Key Vault

cards.statement: Azure Pipelines uses a vault-wide secret selection for a variable group linked to Azure Key Vault.
cards.explanation: A linked variable group keeps an explicit selection of secret names. Adding a vault secret requires updating that selection before the group exposes it.
cards.misconception: Linking a vault makes its full secret inventory available through the variable group.

source.title: Link a variable group to secrets in Azure Key Vault

cards.statement: Azure Pipelines exposes secret variables as script environment variables by default.
cards.explanation: A script task needs an explicit env mapping to receive a secret variable as an environment variable.
cards.misconception: Secret variables receive the same implicit environment-variable mapping as ordinary variables.

cards.statement: Azure Pipelines uses substring matches to mask fragments of secret variable values in task logs.
cards.explanation: Azure Pipelines applies secret masking to full-value matches rather than substrings; a field inside a structured secret can still appear in logs.
cards.misconception: Log masking redacts partial matches of a secret value.

cards.statement: Azure Pipelines automatically deletes the Download secure file task's copy when a failed job finishes.
cards.explanation: The Download secure file task deletes its downloaded copy at job completion, including failed and canceled jobs.

cards.statement: GitHub Actions can sign in to Azure through a federated credential on a Microsoft Entra application.
cards.explanation: The federated credential tells Microsoft Entra ID which GitHub workflow identities it trusts for token exchange.

cards.statement: Azure Pipelines can use system-assigned managed identities for workload identity federation service connections.
cards.explanation: The managed identity option for an Azure Resource Manager workload identity federation service connection uses an existing user-assigned managed identity.
cards.misconception: A federated service connection uses a system-assigned identity like the older agent-assigned authentication option.

source.title: Use an Azure Resource Manager service connection

cards.statement: Azure Pipelines withholds pipeline secrets from GitHub fork pull request builds by default.
cards.explanation: A fork pull request build needs an explicit opt-in to receive pipeline secrets, since a contributor controls its proposed build code.

cards.statement: Azure Pipelines variable groups linked to Azure Key Vault map certificate objects into pipeline variables.
cards.explanation: The variable-group integration maps Azure Key Vault secret objects. It does not map the vault's cryptographic key or certificate objects.
cards.misconception: The variable-group link exposes certificate objects as well as secret objects.

source.title: Link a variable group to secrets in Azure Key Vault

cards.statement: GitHub Advanced Security for Azure DevOps can scan Team Foundation Version Control repositories in Azure Repos.
cards.explanation: GitHub Advanced Security for Azure DevOps covers Azure Repos Git repositories on Azure DevOps Services; TFVC repositories fall outside its scope.
cards.misconception: Advanced Security covers every repository type that Azure Repos hosts.
tags: GitHub Advanced Security for Azure DevOps
cards.volatilityNote: Microsoft could extend the repository types or hosting options that Advanced Security supports.

source.title: Configure GitHub Advanced Security for Azure DevOps features

cards.statement: Turning on GitHub Secret Protection for Azure DevOps in a repository raises alerts for secrets already in its history.
cards.explanation: Turning it on starts repository-level secret scanning, which alerts on existing secrets in historical commits; push protection only evaluates pushes made after enabling.
tags: GitHub Advanced Security for Azure DevOps

source.title: Configure GitHub Advanced Security for Azure DevOps features

cards.statement: GitHub Code Security for Azure DevOps starts dependency scanning once an engineer enables it on a repository.
cards.explanation: Dependency scanning is pipeline-based: it runs in a pipeline with the dependency scanning task or in a repository with dependency scanning default setup, not on enablement alone.
cards.misconception: Enabling the product scans a repository's dependencies by itself.
tags: GitHub Code Security for Azure DevOps

source.title: Set up dependency scanning for GitHub Advanced Security

cards.statement: Microsoft recommends starting Azure Repos code scanning with CodeQL default setup rather than advanced setup.
cards.explanation: Default setup runs CodeQL on a schedule through Azure Pipelines and configures the detected languages itself; teams that need custom build steps, other agent pools or more branches add advanced setup.
tags: GitHub Advanced Security for Azure DevOps

source.title: Configure GitHub Advanced Security for Azure DevOps features

cards.statement: Microsoft Defender for Cloud lists onboarded Azure DevOps, GitHub and GitLab resources in one DevOps inventory.
cards.explanation: DevOps security in Defender for Cloud gives security teams a central view of connected environments, with code, secret, dependency and IaC findings per resource.

source.title: Microsoft Defender for Cloud DevOps security

cards.statement: Defender for Cloud needs engineers to map GitHub repositories to workloads before GHAS findings get runtime context.
cards.explanation: Through the GitHub connector, Defender for Cloud maps repositories to running workloads automatically and raises GHAS findings with risk factors such as internet exposure.
cards.misconception: Code-to-runtime mapping is a manual setup step.
cards.volatilityNote: The GitHub Advanced Security integration with Defender for Cloud is recent and its capabilities can evolve.

source.title: GitHub Advanced Security integration with Microsoft Defender for Cloud

cards.statement: Dependabot can open an alert on an unchanged repository when GitHub adds a matching advisory to its database.
cards.explanation: Dependabot scans the default branch and alerts both when the dependency graph changes and when a new vulnerability enters the GitHub Advisory Database.

cards.statement: Microsoft Defender for Cloud waits until a container image runs in a cluster before assessing its vulnerabilities.
cards.explanation: Registry vulnerability assessment scans images in supported registries such as Azure Container Registry before deployment; runtime assessment adds coverage for running containers.
cards.misconception: Container vulnerability assessment starts at runtime.

cards.statement: CodeQL run outside the container that compiles the code can fail with No source code was seen during the build.
cards.explanation: CodeQL has to monitor a compiled language's build, so GitHub says to run it inside the container in which the code is built, both with the CodeQL CLI and with GitHub Actions.

source.title: Running CodeQL code scanning in a container

cards.statement: Application Insights collects browser page views with its JavaScript SDK rather than OpenTelemetry.
cards.explanation: Browser apps send page views and user interactions through the Application Insights JavaScript SDK, which doesn't use OpenTelemetry; server-side code uses the Azure Monitor OpenTelemetry Distro.

cards.statement: The instrumentation key in an Application Insights connection string authenticates the app's telemetry ingestion.
cards.explanation: The instrumentation key identifies the target resource and is not a security token or key; authenticated ingestion uses Microsoft Entra ID.
cards.misconception: The instrumentation key acts as a secret credential for ingestion.

cards.statement: Azure Monitor Storage insights shows a storage account's capacity once an engineer adds a diagnostic setting.
cards.explanation: Storage insights needs nothing enabled or configured; it uses the storage metrics that Azure collects by default from each storage account.
cards.misconception: Storage insights depends on diagnostic settings to collect its data.

source.title: Monitor Azure Storage services with Azure Monitor Storage insights

cards.statement: Azure Monitor Network Insights topology maps virtual networks and connected resources across subscriptions.
cards.explanation: Topology shows Azure virtual networks, connected resources and their relationships across subscriptions, regions and resource groups, with drill-down to a resource such as a VM.

cards.statement: Azure Monitor managed service for Prometheus can collect AKS container stdout and stderr logs.
cards.explanation: Container log collection uses a containerized Azure Monitor agent to send stdout, stderr and Kubernetes events to Log Analytics; managed Prometheus collects metrics.
cards.misconception: Managed Prometheus collects container logs as well as metrics.

cards.statement: GitHub insights for Projects keeps archived items in a project's historical charts.
cards.explanation: Insights charts use the items in a project as source data and stop tracking items that are archived or deleted.
cards.misconception: Archiving an item preserves it in project insights.

cards.statement: Azure DevOps subscriptions to completed build events offer a filter on the pipeline's definition name.
cards.explanation: The Build completed event exposes fields such as Definition name, Status and Build reason, so a team can be alerted about specific pipelines and outcomes.

cards.statement: An Application Insights standard test checks the SSL certificate of each URL in a redirect chain.
cards.explanation: A standard test follows redirects but validates the SSL certificate on the final redirected URL alone.
cards.misconception: Certificate validation covers every hop of a redirect chain.

cards.statement: A GitHub user can limit GitHub Actions notifications from watched repositories to failed workflow runs.
cards.explanation: The Actions notification setting Only notify for failed workflows delivers workflow run updates when a run fails.

cards.statement: In KQL, requests | where duration > 1000 drops rows whose duration value is null.
cards.explanation: KQL filter comparisons return false for null values, so those rows fail the predicate; functions such as isnull() handle them explicitly.

cards.statement: In KQL, requests | project name, duration returns those two columns followed by the table's other columns.
cards.explanation: project keeps the columns named in its arguments, in that order, and drops every other input column.
cards.misconception: project reorders columns while keeping the rest.

cards.statement: In KQL, requests | summarize count() by timestamp groups the table's rows into hourly bins automatically.
cards.explanation: Automatic hourly bins for datetime columns are no longer supported; summarize count() by bin(timestamp, 1h) groups the rows by hour.
cards.misconception: summarize bins datetime group keys by itself.

cards.statement: In KQL, several ago() calls in one query statement use the same current UTC time.
cards.explanation: Like now(), ago() references one UTC clock value per query statement, so ago(1h) and ago(1d) measure back from the same instant.

cards.statement: In KQL, requests | take 10 returns the ten most recent requests in the table.
cards.explanation: take returns up to the given number of rows with no guarantee which ones unless the data is sorted, and repeated runs can differ.
cards.misconception: take selects the newest rows.

cards.statement: In Application Insights transaction diagnostics, a call between two monitored components appears as two rows.
cards.explanation: One row is the caller's outbound dependency call and the other is the inbound request at the called component; their durations differ by the network round trip.

source.title: Investigate failures, performance, and transactions with Application Insights

cards.statement: Application Insights transaction diagnostics adjusts its Gantt chart timeline for clock skew across component instances.
cards.explanation: The transaction chart corrects timelines for clock skew between instances, while the details pane and Log Analytics keep the exact recorded timestamps.

source.title: Investigate failures, performance, and transactions with Application Insights

cards.statement: Application Insights live metrics stores its streamed data for later queries in Log Analytics.
cards.explanation: Live metrics data persists while it is on the chart and is then discarded; metrics explorer and Log Analytics hold the retained telemetry.
cards.misconception: Live metrics doubles as a retained data store.

source.title: Live metrics: real-time monitoring in Application Insights

cards.statement: The Azure Storage Transactions metric counts failed requests together with successful ones in one total.
cards.explanation: Transactions includes successful requests, failed requests and requests that produced errors; splitting it by the ResponseType dimension separates the kinds of response.

source.title: Azure Blob Storage monitoring data reference
